extracted.intended_audience: computer-science and mathematics researchers (faculty, grad students) writing papers, reports, and books
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance for composing mathematical/computer-science papers, technical reports, survey articles, and books — covering decisions about whether to publish, venue choice, exposition, proof style, sentence/paragraph craft, and revision practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation versus plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't slavishly imitate another's style; imitation becomes culpable plagiarism if a reasonable person could not believe you didn't have the other author's work open while writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot copyright ideas, only expressions. Signs of plagiarism include identical distinctive choices (e.g., identical use of italics) or successive equations lifted verbatim. Even correcting a typo in quoted material can reveal copying. Names were suppressed in notes to protect the guilty — be explicit when quoting to avoid misunderstanding. For survey papers, verbatim quotes are acceptable if the writer does not present the work as their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid bad reasons for writing: (1) to have a long publications list, (2) to have a paper published in a specific conference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish because you have done something you are excited about. Publishing for careerist or venue-driven reasons often yields sloppy work; integrity and quality should govern decisions. Judge yourself also by what you choose not to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Select an appropriate venue based on the maturity and intended audience of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal articles should be polished and timeless; conference papers may be a bit rougher and are appropriate for work 'not yet ready for the archives'; technical reports suit work not ready for general distribution but worth documenting. Always remember there are readers and that a tech report may later become a journal article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edition and revision strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Second and subsequent editions still take significant time but have strong financial advantages and let you reuse earlier examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect roughly a kilohour of effort for a new edition; publishing a new edition can restart sales cycles (people stop buying after ~five years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey papers and verbatim quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey articles may contain lots of verbatim quotes and this is acceptable because the author is not presenting the quoted material as their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, be explicit in your quotation. Accusations of plagiarism often hinge on financial loss, and technical papers are usually not written primarily for money, but clarity about sources avoids problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of analogy and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use analogy, metaphor, and simile where they help readers understand the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CS exposition uses less analogy than physics perhaps due to subject nature; use analogy when you are sure the reader will get the point; beware letting the conceit intrude on content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceit and thematic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceit (a fanciful organizing idea) can catalyze writing but should not be allowed to intrude or persist if it stops serving clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to abandon the conceit; the line between useful conceit and merely cute is fine. Beware of jokes — humor may age poorly (ten years later it might not work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor concrete examples: one solid example is better than a dry abstract paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple examples are never a mistake (especially for lectures). Examples keep you honest — if your theory can't handle the example you planned to use, revise the theory. Examples can expose weaknesses and force improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure before formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on structure, not formatting, during writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't think about formatting when composing; think about structure. Use macros for complex notation rather than writing it out verbatim. Structural forms (e.g., tabular proofs) can clarify ideas — formatting choices should follow structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof presentation: tabular vs paragraph style
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 'statement–reason' (tabular) form to clarify the structure of proofs, and then present paragraph proofs informed by that structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tabular proofs are often easier to read and help clarify logical steps; they are not about cosmetics but enforcing structure. Producing a tabular proof can reveal bloated prose and allow trimming.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence and opening
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence should be nontechnical, exciting, simple, direct, and represent the author's best effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid passive 'wimpiness' in openings. The first sentence should 'leap out' and then the second must not disappoint. Maintain that energy throughout the paper — keep 'socking it to them' by sustaining quality through all sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice ('passive wimpiness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active, direct constructions over passive ones to produce stronger writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport admonishes to 'avoid passive wimpiness' — be simple and direct. Active sentences help make first sentences and key statements more compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix ideas before sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad writing often stems from bad thinking; don't merely 'fix the sentence and not the idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on clarity of thought and structure first; polishing superficial sentence details cannot rescue unclear ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to write by reading broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Study great literature to learn how to write good mathematical/scientific prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading widely (including literature) sharpens style and critical faculties; pay homage to strong writers while learning varied techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-management maxim
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't spend more than a year on anything (Lamport's maxim as presented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat projects with time constraints to avoid endless reworking; recognize when to stop and move on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and rewriting discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite repeatedly — 'Write, rewrite, rewrite...' — as fundamental to producing good work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most artists repeatedly labor over their work; expect to discard many drafts. Solicit critiques and be prepared to revise after external feedback (examples: Karnaugh pointed out a flaw leading to corrections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Get external critiques before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Never publish without having had others critique your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A university environment is useful to obtain feedback, but time requests carefully. Use knowledgeable readers to catch oversights you missed (as in examples where colleagues found derivation errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader (reader primitives and 'daemons')
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly imagine the reader's knowledge and potential misunderstandings; develop internal checks ('daemons') that flag errors automatically as you write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'How is the reader going to misunderstand me here?' and run many background checks (style, grammar, technical assumptions). Over time these checks should run automatically to keep writing fun rather than compulsive rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium (vocabulary, typography, visuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire a good vocabulary and mastery of non-textual tools: indexes, tables, graphs, typography, and appropriate fonts for formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good vocabulary needn't be huge; learn how to use typographic conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logical formulae) and use visuals effectively. Anticipate changing media (interactive reading/writing) and adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material (writing to understand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing organizes thought and often leads to better understanding; use lectures, talks, and teaching to refine your internal model of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use writing as a tool to teach yourself; expect to discover issues or change your thinking while organizing material for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify initially; use the 80-20 rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin exposition with simplified accounts or examples; it's acceptable to defer some correct details until later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present straightforward starts even if you 'bend the facts' initially and pay back by gradual elaboration. Using simple examples can convey most of the idea with less difficulty; avoid terseness that sacrifices reader accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling old material verbatim
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist reusing previous material unchanged because context and emphasis change; rewrite old text to fit the new context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite tempting convenience with on-line text and editors, rewrite because you're likely a different (older, wiser) writer and the new context demands fresh exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for excellence (continual improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always strive for the best possible work; 'good' should not be enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the mindset of perpetual apprenticeship — keep shooting for perfection even if unattainable; demand high standards in all aspects of writing and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual-labor composition exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manual practices (typing/copying by hand, memorization, recitation) to slow down and deepen engagement with text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying text helps you read closely; memorization/recitation trains word-by-word sensitivity. These manual techniques may feel odd but can strengthen composition skills (e.g., type passages to understand them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level syntactic metrics and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor sentence length averages and variation as a proxy for syntactic fitness: target ~15–18 words average and high variation across sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary‑Claire's technique: sample first 10 complete sentences on page three; adults should average ≥20 words? (she suggests under 20 words per sentence is correct range), ideal bell-curve centered 15–18 words. In 10 sentences aim for 9–10 different lengths; avoid too many identical templates (e.g., adverbial+subject+verb+object repeated). Use a few short punchy sentences and occasional long ones for emphasis control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tight parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two adjacent sentences with exactly the same construction (tight parallels) to communicate similarity effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight parallels are an effective rhetorical device; note when you avoid or overuse them. Be aware they may be underused by some writers and can enhance clarity when used intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentences as a high literary form
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize periodic sentences (where grammatical and physical ends coincide) as a high literary form, generally inappropriate for technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding periodic sentences increases control over sentence structure, but reserve them for literary effects rather than typical research exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphatic sentence positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Front and back positions of a sentence are the primary emphatic positions; vary sentence structure to shift emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice recasting sentences to test emphasis — 'the middle of a sentence is sort of a slum.' Use position deliberately to emphasize or deemphasize points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense-stream cohesion exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice writing an unrelated stream of thoughts glued together with linking words ('thus', 'therefore', etc.) to hone cohesion skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This playful exercise helps train connective tissue of exposition; Mary‑Claire recommends it as fun practice (maybe after a couple of drinks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud, form partnerships, and get oral feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your writing aloud to partners and listen to their reactions; form critique partnerships but limit exposure if writing is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud highlights 'frozen sounds' and cadence; partnerships let you taste and hear prose. A little feedback can go a long way; sustained poor writing can be hard to endure collectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks-on-paper and iterative drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat writing as a forgiving, iterative medium — mark up drafts and revise until the meaning is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E. M. Forster: 'How do I know what I mean till I see what I say?' Use the manuscript as a tool for discovery and correction; iterate until the text says what you intend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance, voice, and tone: exaggeration exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Use speech-therapy-like exaggeration to understand defects in stance, voice, and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate a reported defect (e.g., 'breezy') by writing something extreme to understand and correct it later. This diagnostic helps you detect and control stylistic issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion and verse practice for technical writers
rubrics_metrics.description: Scansion and verse-writing exercises are hard but useful for improving rhythm and control in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though counterintuitive, learning verse can improve prose rhythm and sensitivity to cadence; Mary‑Claire recommends trusting the technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Précis exercise and structural reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing word count (précis) eventually forces structural changes; you should preserve meaning while dispensing with details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At some percentage of reduction you cannot just cut words without altering structure. The goal is to keep meaning intact while reorganizing content to be more concise; the required structural change depends on the 'flabbiness' of the original.
